assignment.title: Algebra II Honors — Operations with Radical Expressions
assignment.essentialQuestion: Why can it be useful to simplify expressions?
assignment.instructions: Operations with radical expressions. Each multi-step question has a box for every step — the perfect-power factor, each FOIL product, the conjugate — and each step is checked, so show the work in the boxes. You have 3 tries on each Warm-Up, Classwork and Practice question, with hints. The Exit Ticket is one try with no hints.
assignment.teacherNotes: Algebra II Honors, Radicals Lesson 2 (Operations with Radical Expressions), from the district slides, TEKS A2.7G. Warm-Up rebuilt as readiness: a Lesson 1 root, like terms → like radicals, and (x + a)(x − a) → conjugates. Classwork follows every slide example and Check Your Progress, staged so each step is a graded box. "Simplify" answers are graded by value AND form (simplest radical form). Changes from the slides: the four simplest-form rules (CW4) come before the Quotient Property items that ask for simplest form; the slides’ Check Your Progress B, ⁴√(625b²⁸k²³) with b any real number, is CW9, an extension after multiplying radicals, and CW3 checks Example B with a cube root, every variable positive; Practice opens with the simplest rationalization (P1). Two audited Digital SAT items from the CCMR bank sit in Practice; P7, P8, P10, P11 and P12 are the Honors extension (DOK 3–4), so the Honors version is ready as written. Warm-Up and Exit Ticket are generated per student and back Recovery.

questions.prompt: Lesson 1 review. Simplify $\sqrt[3]{ -{{c3}}a^{ {{e1}} }y^{ {{e2}} } }$.
directionSteps: Write the radicand as a cube.
Take the cube root and keep its sign.
hints: Which number, cubed, gives {{c3}}? What power of a, cubed, gives a^{{e1}}?
{{c3}} = {{c}}³ and each exponent divides by 3. An odd root of a negative number is negative.

misconceptions.message: An odd root keeps the sign of its radicand: the cube root of a negative number is negative.

steps.title: Odd index
steps.instruction: An odd root keeps the sign: ∛(−8) = −2.

solutionReview.headline: Write a cube; the odd root keeps the sign.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing the cube root of the coefficient as a third of it.

questions.prompt: Like terms become like radicals. Combine like terms in $ {{a}}x - {{b}}x + {{c}}x $. Then combine $ {{d}}\sqrt{ {{k}} } + {{e}}\sqrt{ {{k}} } $ the same way.
directionSteps: Combine the like terms in the first expression.
Combine the radicals in the second expression the same way.
hints: What do the three terms have in common? What do the two radicals have in common?
Like terms keep their common part and add their coefficients. Radicals with the same index and radicand are like terms too.

steps.title: Like radical expressions
steps.instruction: Same index and same radicand: 3√5 and −8√5 are like radicals, but √5 and ∛5 are not.

solutionReview.headline: Add the coefficients; keep the common part.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding the radicands too: √{{k}} + √{{k}} is 2√{{k}}, not √(2 · {{k}}).

questions.prompt: Conjugates. Multiply $(x + {{a}})(x - {{a}})$. Then multiply $(\sqrt{ {{k}} } + {{a}})(\sqrt{ {{k}} } - {{a}})$ the same way. What happens to the radical?
directionSteps: Multiply the first pair of binomials.
Multiply the second pair the same way.
Decide what happens to the radical.

responses.label: The product has no radical because…
options: radicals always cancel when you multiply two binomials
the square root of {{a}} is a whole number, so no radical is left

hints: What are the four products when you multiply the two binomials?
The two middle products are opposites. What do they add to?
A square root times itself is its radicand, so no radical is left.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (a + b)(a − b) equals…

steps.title: Conjugates
steps.instruction: a + b and a − b are conjugates: their product is a² − b². With a square root in a or b, the product has no radical.

solutionReview.headline: Difference of squares: the middle terms cancel.
solutionReview.commonError: Forgetting that √{{k}} · √{{k}} = {{k}} and leaving a radical in the answer.

questions.prompt: Like radical expressions. Sort each expression: after you simplify it, can it be combined with √5, or not? Give a reason for each group.
directionSteps: Simplify each expression.
Decide whether it can be combined with the given radical.
Give a reason for each group.
hints: Once each card is simplified, does it have the same index and the same radicand as √5?
Which perfect square can you pull out of √20, √45, √50 and √80?
A cube root is never a like radical with a square root, and √(5x) has a different radicand.

steps.title: Like radical expressions
steps.instruction: Same index AND same radicand: 4√3, −√3 and 2√3 are like; √3 and ∛3 are not, and neither are √3 and √(3x).

steps.title: Simplify first
steps.instruction: √12 = 2√3, so √12 is a like radical with √3 even though it does not look like one.

solutionReview.headline: Simplify, then compare index and radicand.
reasoning: √20 = 2√5, 2√45 = 6√5 and √80 = 4√5, so they combine with √5, as do 3√5 and −√5.
∛5 has a different index; 5√3 has radicand 3; √50 = 5√2 has radicand 2; √(5x) has radicand 5x.
solutionReview.commonError: Sorting √20 as unlike: simplified, it is 2√5.

questions.prompt: Product Property, Examples A and B. Simplify $\sqrt{25a^4b^9}$ and $\sqrt[3]{125m^{30}p^{20}}$. Assume every variable is positive. Factor each radicand into a perfect power and what is left.
directionSteps: Find the perfect-square factor of the first radicand.
Simplify the first radical.
Find the perfect-cube factor of the second radicand.
Simplify the second radical.
hints: Which exponents in 25a⁴b⁹ are even? Which in 125m³⁰p²⁰ are multiples of 3?
For a square root, use the largest even exponent of each letter; for a cube root, the largest multiple of 3.
b⁹ = b⁸ · b and p²⁰ = p¹⁸ · p². Take the root of the perfect-power factor; what is left stays under the radical.

steps.title: Product Property of Radicals
steps.instruction: ⁿ√(ab) = ⁿ√a · ⁿ√b if n is even and a and b are nonnegative, or if n is odd. √2 · √8 = √16 = 4 and ∛3 · ∛9 = ∛27 = 3.

solutionReview.headline: Perfect power out, the rest stays in.
solutionReview.commonError: Dividing the exponent 20 by 3 and writing p^(20/3) outside: only p¹⁸ = (p⁶)³ comes out; p² stays in.

questions.prompt: Check Your Progress A and B. Simplify $\sqrt{16x^4y^{11}}$ and $\sqrt[3]{27x^9y^{14}}$. Assume every variable is positive.
directionSteps: Simplify the square root.
Simplify the cube root.
hints: What is the largest even exponent of y up to 11? The largest multiple of 3 up to 14?
y¹¹ is not a perfect square and y¹⁴ is not a perfect cube, so a power of y stays under each radical.
Take the root of the perfect-power factor; what is left stays under the radical.

misconceptions.message: Check what stays under the cube root: y¹⁴ is y¹² times what?

solutionReview.headline: As in the examples: perfect power out, the rest stays in.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing 3x³y⁴∛y: y¹⁴ = y¹² · y², so y², not y, stays under the cube root.

questions.prompt: Simplest form. A radical expression is simplified when the index is as small as possible, the radicand has no perfect nth-power factor, the radicand has no fraction, and no radical is in a denominator. Decide whether each expression is in simplest form, and name the rule it breaks if it is not.
directionSteps: Check each expression against the four rules.
Decide whether it is simplified.
Name the rule it breaks, if any.

options: Not simplified: 12 has a perfect-square factor
Simplified: 12 is not a perfect square
Not simplified: a fraction is under the radical
Not simplified: the index can be smaller
responses.answer: Not simplified: 12 has a perfect-square factor

options: Not simplified: a radical is in the denominator
Not simplified: 5 has a perfect-square factor
Not simplified: the index of √5 can be smaller
responses.answer: Not simplified: a radical is in the denominator

responses.label: ⁶√(x²)
options: Not simplified: the index can be smaller
Simplified: x² has no perfect sixth-power factor
Not simplified: a radical is in the denominator
Not simplified: a fraction is under the radical
responses.answer: Not simplified: the index can be smaller

responses.label: √(x/2)
options: Not simplified: a fraction is under the radical
Simplified: x and 2 have no perfect-square factor
Not simplified: the index can be smaller
Not simplified: x has a perfect-square factor
responses.answer: Not simplified: a fraction is under the radical

responses.label: 2∛(3x²)
options: Not simplified: x² is a perfect square
Not simplified: the index can be smaller
Not simplified: a radical is in the denominator

responses.label: Write ⁶√(x²) as a radical in simplest form (x positive)

hints: For each expression, which of the four rules does it break, if any?
A radical in a numerator is fine; a radical in a denominator is not. Can ⁶√(x²) be written with a smaller index?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Is √3/3 in simplest form?

solutionReview.headline: Four rules, one at a time.
reasoning: ⁶√(x²) = ∛x (smaller index). √(x/2) = √(2x)/2 (fraction under the radical). 2∛(3x²) breaks no rule.
solutionReview.answerSummary: a, b, c, d not simplified; e simplified; ⁶√(x²) = ∛x
solutionReview.commonError: Calling 2∛(3x²) unsimplified: neither 3 nor x² contains a perfect cube.

questions.prompt: Quotient Property, Example A. Simplify $\sqrt{\dfrac{y^8}{x^7}}$. Assume $x$ and $y$ are positive. Split the root over the numerator and the denominator, simplify each, then rationalize the denominator.
directionSteps: Simplify the root of the denominator.
Rationalize the denominator.
Write the simplified quotient.

responses.label: To clear the radical from x³√x, the smallest radical to multiply the top and bottom by is

hints: What is the largest even exponent of x up to 7?
Split the root over the top and the bottom. What can you multiply by so no radical is left in the denominator?
x⁷ = (x³)² · x, and a square root times itself equals its radicand.

steps.title: Quotient Property of Radicals
steps.instruction: ⁿ√(a/b) = ⁿ√a / ⁿ√b if all roots are defined. √27/√3 = √9 = 3.

steps.title: Rationalizing the denominator
steps.instruction: Multiply the numerator and denominator by the radical that makes the denominator a perfect power.

solutionReview.headline: Split, simplify, rationalize.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at y⁴/(x³√x): a radical may not stay in a denominator.

questions.prompt: Quotient Property, Example B. Simplify $\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{2}{9x}}$. Assume $x$ is positive. Find what to multiply $9x$ by to make a perfect cube, then simplify.
directionSteps: Find what makes the denominator a perfect cube.
Multiply and simplify the cube root of the new denominator.
Write the simplified quotient.

responses.label: Multiply 9x by ? to get a perfect cube
The new radicand in the denominator

hints: What do you multiply 9 by to get a perfect cube? And x?
A perfect cube has a coefficient that is a cube and every exponent a multiple of 3. Multiply the numerator by the same cube root.
9x · 3x² = 27x³ = (3x)³, so multiply the top and bottom by ∛(3x²).

misconceptions.message: 9x · 9x = 81x², which is not a perfect cube.
9x · 9x = 81x², which is not a perfect cube.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which is a perfect cube?

solutionReview.headline: Build a perfect cube in the denominator.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying by ∛(9x)/∛(9x): 9x · 9x = 81x² is not a perfect cube.

questions.prompt: Check Your Progress A and B. Simplify $\sqrt{\dfrac{x^3}{y^7}}$ and $\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{8}{3y^2}}$. Assume $x$ and $y$ are positive.
directionSteps: Simplify the first quotient.
Find the multiplier for the second denominator.
Simplify the second quotient.

responses.label: Multiply 3y² by ? to get a perfect cube

hints: For the first, what are √(x³) and √(y⁷) with the perfect squares taken out?
Clear the √y left in the denominator. For the second: 3y² times what gives (3y)³?
√(x³) = x√x and √(y⁷) = y³√y; multiply the top and bottom by √y. ∛8 is a whole number.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. To rationalize 1/(y³√y), multiply by…

solutionReview.headline: Split, simplify, rationalize.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at x√x/(y³√y): it still has a radical in the denominator.

questions.prompt: Multiply radicals. Simplify $5\sqrt[3]{100a^2}\cdot\sqrt[3]{10a}$, then $3\sqrt[3]{16a^2}\cdot 2\sqrt[3]{4a}$.
directionSteps: Multiply the radicands of the first product.
Take the cube root and multiply.
Simplify the second product the same way.
hints: How can you write a product of two cube roots as one cube root?
Multiply the radicands. Is the product a perfect cube: a cube number times a³?
∛m · ∛n = ∛(mn). Keep the coefficients: for the second, multiply 3 and 2 too.

misconceptions.message: That is the cube root alone: keep the coefficient 5 in front.
The coefficients multiply too: keep both 3 and 2 in front.

solutionReview.headline: One radical, a perfect cube, then the coefficients.
solutionReview.commonError: Forgetting the outside coefficients after taking the cube root.

questions.prompt: Extension — the Product Property with an even index. Simplify $\sqrt[4]{625b^{28}k^{23}}$, where $b$ can be any real number. Explain why only $b^7$ needs absolute value bars.
directionSteps: Simplify the fourth root.
Explain why only one factor needs bars.

responses.label: Why does b⁷ need bars but k⁵ does not?
options: b⁷ is negative when b is; k is under an even root, so k ≥ 0
b has the larger exponent, so b⁷ is the factor that can be negative
b⁷ is negative when b is; k⁵ needs bars too, but they are not written
Only the first variable outside an even root ever needs bars
responses.answer: b⁷ is negative when b is; k is under an even root, so k ≥ 0

hints: Which number to the fourth power is 625? What is the largest multiple of 4 up to 28? Up to 23?
b can be negative, so which factor needs bars? For k²³ to have a real fourth root, can k be negative?
625 = 5⁴, b²⁸ = (b⁷)⁴ and k²³ = (k⁵)⁴ · k³. Only b⁷ can be negative.

misconceptions.message: Your answer is right when b ≥ 0. Try b = −1.
The fourth root of 625 is not 625 ÷ 5.

solutionReview.headline: Pull out the largest perfect power; bars only where a factor can be negative.
reasoning: 625b²⁸k²³ = (5b⁷k⁵)⁴ · k³, so the root is |5b⁷k⁵| ⁴√(k³) = 5|b⁷|k⁵ · ⁴√(k³): k ≥ 0 for the radicand to be real.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing 125|b⁷|…: the fourth root of 625 is 5, not 625 ÷ 5.

questions.prompt: Add and subtract radicals. Simplify $3\sqrt{45} - 5\sqrt{80} + 4\sqrt{20}$ by simplifying each term first. Then simplify $3\sqrt{75} - 2\sqrt{48} + \sqrt{3}$.
directionSteps: Simplify each term of the first expression.
Combine the like radicals.
Simplify the second expression the same way.
hints: What is the largest perfect square that divides 45? 80? 20?
Once every term is a multiple of √5, add and subtract the coefficients, keeping each sign with its term.
45 = 9 · 5, 80 = 16 · 5 and 20 = 4 · 5. Do the same for 75 and 48.

misconceptions.message: Keep each sign with its term: the middle term is subtracted.
Only like radicals combine: simplify each radical first, then combine the coefficients.

steps.title: Combine like radicals
steps.instruction: Simplify every radical first; then add or subtract the coefficients of like radicals.

solutionReview.headline: Simplify each term, then combine.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding radicands: √45 − √80 + √20 is not √(45 − 80 + 20).

questions.prompt: Multiply binomials with radicals (FOIL). Simplify $(2\sqrt{3} + 3\sqrt{5})(3 - \sqrt{3})$ one product at a time. Then simplify $(2\sqrt{5} + 4\sqrt{6})(5 - \sqrt{7})$.
directionSteps: Find the first, outer, inner and last products.
Write the sum.
Multiply the second pair the same way.
hints: Which four products does FOIL give? Name the first, outer, inner and last pairs.
What is √3 · √3? What is √5 · √3?
√3 · √3 = 3 and √5 · √3 = √15. Unlike radicals stay as separate terms.

misconceptions.message: FOIL gives four products: first, outer, inner and last. Check that your answer has all four.

solutionReview.headline: Four products, then combine only like terms.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing 2√3 · (−√3) = −2√9 and stopping: √9 is 3, so the product is −6.

questions.prompt: GEOMETRY — use a conjugate. In a square with side $a$, the ratio of a side to the difference between the diagonal and a side is $\dfrac{a}{a\sqrt{2} - a}$. Rationalize the denominator and simplify. Then, in the triangle with height $x$ and base $x\sqrt{3} + x$, simplify the ratio of the height to the base, $\dfrac{x}{x\sqrt{3} + x}$.
directionSteps: Name the conjugate of the first denominator.
Multiply the first denominator by its conjugate.
Simplify the first ratio.
Simplify the second ratio.

responses.label: The conjugate of a√2 − a is

hints: What do you change in a√2 − a to get its conjugate?
A conjugate pair multiplies to a difference of squares. What is (a√2)²?
(a√2)² − a² = 2a² − a². Factor out the common factor a (or x) and cancel it.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The conjugate of √3 + 1 is…

steps.title: Conjugate
steps.instruction: a√b + c√d and a√b − c√d are conjugates. Multiplying a binomial denominator by its conjugate clears the radical.

solutionReview.headline: Multiply by the conjugate, then cancel the common factor.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying by (a√2 − a)/(a√2 − a): that squares the denominator and keeps the radical.

sections.title: Practice — Radical Operations, with Honors Extension and College-Readiness

questions.prompt: Rationalize the denominator: simplify $\dfrac{ {{a}} }{\sqrt{ {{m}} }}$.
directionSteps: Multiply the top and bottom by the radical in the denominator.
Simplify.
hints: What can you multiply √{{m}} by to get a whole number?
Multiply the top and the bottom by √{{m}}: a square root times itself is its radicand.

misconceptions.message: Multiplying only the bottom by √{{m}} changes the value: multiply the top by √{{m}} too.

solutionReview.headline: Multiply by √{{m}}/√{{m}}.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying only the denominator by √{{m}}, which changes the value.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt[3]{ {{R}}m^{ {{e}} } }$.
directionSteps: Find the largest perfect-cube factor.
Take its cube root outside the radical.
Keep what is left under the radical.
hints: Which perfect cube divides {{R}}? What is the largest multiple of 3 up to {{e}}?
{{R}} = {{c}}³ · {{k}}: take the cube root of the perfect cube, and use the largest exponent of m that is a multiple of 3.

solutionReview.headline: Perfect cube out, the rest in.
solutionReview.commonError: Taking a square root of the powers instead of a cube root.

directionSteps: Simplify each term.
Combine the like radicals.
hints: What is the largest perfect square that divides each radicand?
Each radicand is a perfect square times {{k}}. Simplify each term, then combine the coefficients, keeping each sign.

solutionReview.headline: Simplify each term, then combine.
solutionReview.commonError: Combining the radicands before simplifying.

questions.prompt: Simplify ${{c1}}\sqrt[3]{ {{u}}a^2 }\cdot {{c2}}\sqrt[3]{ {{w}}a }$.
directionSteps: Multiply the radicands.
Take the cube root.
Multiply by the coefficients.
hints: How can you write the product of the two cube roots as one cube root?
Multiply the radicands: the product is a perfect cube. Then multiply by the coefficients {{c1}} and {{c2}}.

misconceptions.message: That is the cube root alone: multiply it by the coefficients {{c1}} and {{c2}} too.

solutionReview.headline: One radical, a perfect cube, then the coefficients.
solutionReview.commonError: Forgetting the coefficients {{c1}} and {{c2}}.

questions.prompt: Simplify $({{p}} + {{q|coef}}\sqrt{ {{m}} })({{r}} + {{s|coef}}\sqrt{ {{m}} })$.
directionSteps: Find the four products.
Combine the whole numbers and the like radicals.
hints: Which four products does FOIL give?
What is a radical times itself? Which two products are like radicals?
A radical times itself is its radicand, and the two middle products combine into one radical term.

solutionReview.headline: FOIL, then combine like terms.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving the last product as a radical instead of a whole number.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt{ {{R}}a^{ {{e1}} }b^{ {{e2}} } }$. Assume $a$ and $b$ are positive.
directionSteps: Find the largest perfect-square factor.
Take its square root outside the radical.
Keep what is left under the radical.
hints: Which perfect square divides {{R}}? What is the largest even exponent of b up to {{e2}}?
{{R}} = {{s}}² · {{k}}: take the square root of the perfect square, and use the largest even exponent of b; one b stays inside.

solutionReview.headline: Perfect square out, the rest in.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving a perfect-square factor of {{R}} under the radical.

questions.prompt: Use a conjugate: simplify $\dfrac{ {{a}} }{ {{b}} + \sqrt{ {{m}} } }$.
directionSteps: Multiply the denominator by its conjugate.
Multiply the numerator by the same conjugate.
Simplify.
hints: What is the conjugate of the denominator?
Multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate: the denominator becomes a difference of squares with no radical.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The conjugate of 4 + √3 is…

solutionReview.headline: Multiply by the conjugate over itself.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying by √{{m}}/√{{m}}: the denominator still has a radical.

questions.prompt: GEOMETRY. In a square with side $a$, the ratio of the diagonal to the sum of the diagonal and a side is $\dfrac{a\sqrt{2}}{a\sqrt{2} + a}$. Simplify the ratio.
directionSteps: Cancel the common factor.
Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator.
Simplify.
hints: What factor do all three terms share?
Cancel that factor. What do you multiply the top and bottom by to clear the radical from the denominator?
Multiply the top and bottom by √2 − 1: (√2 + 1)(√2 − 1) has no radical.

solutionReview.headline: Cancel, then use the conjugate.
solutionReview.commonError: Cancelling the √2 in the numerator with the √2 in the denominator: only common FACTORS cancel.

questions.prompt: Error analysis. Maya writes $\sqrt{16x} + \sqrt{9x} = \sqrt{25x} = 5\sqrt{x}$. Assume $x$ is positive. Test the rule $\sqrt{a + b} = \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}$ with $a = 9$ and $b = 16$, explain Maya's error, and simplify correctly.
directionSteps: Find the value of the left side of the rule.
Find the value of the right side.
Explain the error.
Simplify correctly.

responses.label: Maya’s error:
options: She added the radicands; like radicals add by their coefficients
Her answer is right: radicals add by adding their radicands
She forgot bars: √x needs |x|, because x could be negative
She should have multiplied the coefficients: 4 · 3√x = 12√x
responses.answer: She added the radicands; like radicals add by their coefficients

hints: Does √(a + b) = √a + √b hold for a = 9 and b = 16? Work out each side.
Simplify each radical first: each one is a whole number times √x.

misconceptions.message: That is Maya’s answer: √(16x) + √(9x) is not √(25x).

solutionReview.headline: Radicals do not add like radicands.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing √(a + b) = √a + √b: a counterexample shows it is false.

questions.prompt: Honors extension — compare without a calculator. Order $3\sqrt{5}$, $2\sqrt{11}$ and $5\sqrt{2}$ from least to greatest. Square each number to compare, and justify your order.
directionSteps: Square each number.
Order the numbers.
Justify the order.

responses.label: Why does comparing the squares work?
options: For positive numbers, the larger number has the larger square
For any numbers, the larger number has the larger square
Only the coefficients matter, and squaring keeps them in order
Squaring reverses the order of positive numbers, so read it backward
responses.answer: For positive numbers, the larger number has the larger square

hints: How do you square a number like 3√5: what happens to the 3, and to the √5?
(a√b)² = a² · b, and squaring keeps the order of positive numbers.

solutionReview.headline: Square, compare, and order.
reasoning: 44 < 45 < 50, and squaring keeps the order of positive numbers, so 2√11 < 3√5 < 5√2.
solutionReview.commonError: Ordering by the coefficients alone (2, 3, 5) or by the radicands alone.

questions.prompt: Honors extension — model with conjugates. A landscaper designs three rectangular garden beds whose length and width (in meters) are conjugates, as the table shows. Find each area and the perimeter of bed C, then explain why every area is a whole number.
directionSteps: Multiply each length by its width.
Find the perimeter of bed C.
Explain why every area is a whole number.

responses.label: Every area is a whole number because…
options: length and width are conjugates, so their product has no radical
radicals always multiply to whole numbers, so any length times width does
the widths are whole numbers, and a whole number times a radical is whole
length and width are conjugates, so their sum has no radical
responses.answer: length and width are conjugates, so their product has no radical

hints: Each length and width are a + b and a − b. What is their product?
How do you square 2√3? Square the 2 and the √3 separately.
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b², and (2√3)² = 4 · 3. Perimeter = 2 · length + 2 · width.

misconceptions.message: (2√3)² is not 2 · 3: square the 2 as well.

solutionReview.headline: Conjugates multiply to a difference of squares.

questions.prompt: Honors extension — cube-root denominators. Simplify $\dfrac{6}{\sqrt[3]{4}}$ and $\dfrac{10}{\sqrt[3]{25}}$.
directionSteps: Find what makes each denominator a perfect cube.
Multiply and simplify.

responses.label: Multiply the first fraction by ? over itself

hints: What do you multiply 4 by to get a perfect cube? And 25?
Multiply the top and the bottom by the same cube root, so the denominator is the cube root of a perfect cube.
4 · 2 = 8 and 25 · 5 = 125 are perfect cubes. Reduce the fraction at the end.

solutionReview.headline: Build a perfect cube under the denominator.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying by ∛4/∛4: 4 · 4 = 16 is not a perfect cube.

questions.prompt: For $x\ge0$, which expression is equivalent to $\sqrt{{{a2}}x}+\sqrt{{{b2}}x}$?

optionRationales.${{sum}}\\sqrt{x}$: Right: √({{a2}}x) = {{a}}√x and √({{b2}}x) = {{b}}√x, and like radicals add by their coefficients.
optionRationales.${{prod}}\\sqrt{x}$: This multiplies the coefficients {{a}} and {{b}}. Like radicals are added by adding their coefficients.
optionRationales.${{a}}x+{{b}}x$: This takes x out of the roots too. x is not a perfect square, so √x stays; only {{a2}} and {{b2}} come out.
